 Why Your 2.8% Social Security COLA Is Losing Ground Fast
 John Csiszar 2026년 11월 4일 수 오후 5:00 UTC 0 Delmaine Donson · iStock.com Every January, the Social Security Administration enacts a cost-of-living adjustment for beneficiaries to help them keep up with rising costs. But for 2026, the COLA was just 2.8%, boosting the average retired worker’s check by about $56 per month.
 Inflationary pressures have eaten up all of that increase for many retirees due to these primary factors.

 Take Action: 9 Low-Effort Ways To Make Passive Income (You Can Start This Week) 
 Medicare's Part B Premium Outpaced Inflation
 Per the Federal Register , the standard monthly Medicare Part B premium for 2026 is $202.90. That’s an increase of $17.90 from 2025’s $185, or a nearly 10% jump. Part B premiums now consume roughly 32% of 2026’s entire COLA, leaving just $38.10 in monthly spending power from the $56 increase.
 The Medicare Deductible Also Popped
 The Federal Register also notes that the Part B annual deductible for 2026 is $283, up $26 from 2025's $257. That's an out-of-pocket expense that is paid in addition to the regular monthly premium for those who actually use care. In some cases, even a single visit to a doctor will end up costing $26 more than it would have in 2025, taking another bite out of the Social Security COLA increase.
 Inflation Is Running Hotter Than the COLA Increase
 Over the 12 months ending July 2026, the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers increased 3.4%, per the Bureau of Labor Statistics . That's higher than the 2.8% COLA raise that retirees received starting in January.
 Advertisement
 Part of the reason for the discrepancy is timing. The COLA is calculated in the third quarter of the prior year, long before COLA-adjusted payments actually go out. By the time retirees get their checks, the current inflation rate could potentially be higher than the COLA rate, which is based on data that's already several months old by the time it takes effect.
 Retirees are particularly sensitive to shelter costs, including rent and homeownership expenses. As of July 2026, the BLS reported that expenses in that category rose by 3.2%, above the 2.8% cost-of-living adjustment for 2026. For seniors looking for Social Security to help ease their housing costs, the exact opposite happened.
 The COLA Is Based on a Different Index
 The CPI-W population represents working-age wage earners and clerical workers, according to the Social Security Administration . This demographic can have significantly different spending patterns than retirees, who are generally more affected by housing, healthcare and long-term care costs. This means that the index calculating the raise isn't actually built around the spending pattern of the people receiving it.
 For example, BLS data shows that households aged 75 and older devote 16% of their total spending to healthcare, compared with just 3.8% for households under 25. But the CPI-W is skewed towards a younger population that underweights the cost of healthcare relative to seniors. This can lead to a mismatch in pricing between the COLA and the rising costs seniors actually absorb.
 The Senior Citizens League projects that the 2027 COLA, which will be announced in October 2026, will be 3.6%. This estimate can vary at any time but amounts to a nice bump over the 2.8% retirees received in 2026. But whether it’s enough to truly cover the increased cost of living for seniors depends on what prices do between now and then.
